Psychological Operations (PSYOPs), previously identified as Military Information Support Operations (MISO), funds the operational employment of
PSYOP to change the behavior of foreign target audiences to meet Department of War (DoW) objectives. These funds are distributed to, and
executed by, the Combatant Commands (CCMD). The interconnectedness of global communication systems and the ability of our adversaries to
use information trans-regionally requires the DoW to compete in the information domain at a strategic level.
The FY 2027 request of $325,609 thousand reflects the Department’s approach to PSYOP budgeting by utilizing a central fund within the Office of
the Secretary of War (OSW). The Office of the Assistant Secretary of War for Special Operations and Low Intensity Conflict (OASW(SO/LIC)) is
responsible for PSYOP program management and budget formulation. A single PSYOP account increases transparency and enhances
OASW(SO/LIC) oversight of PSYOP programming; FY 2027 represents the fifth year of the Department’s utilization of a consolidated PSYOP budget
to fund PSYOP operations and the fourth year the Department used a PSYOP Resource Request (PRR) process managed by OASW(SO/LIC) to
prioritize and allocate resources amongst CCMDs.
The PSYOP program continues to use one program project code (Execution) as approved in FY 2024 which allows for better management and
oversight of the program, better execution definitions, and easier congressional reporting.
These funds resource the operational employment of PSYOP to change the behavior of foreign target audiences and encompasses PSYOP
planning, execution, assessment, and support. This includes the planning, analysis, production, translation, distribution, and dissemination costs
associated with providing information to foreign audiences, through a variety of communication mechanisms (audio, visual, and audio-visual),
designed to affect the foreign audiences' perceptions, reasoning, beliefs, motivations, decisions, and ultimately behavior. These funds are
distributed to all Combatant Commands for requirements associated with PSYOP and utilized in accordance with DoW policies for PSYOP fund
expenditures. These funds also include necessary travel expenses of civilian full-time equivalents (FTE) and contractor FTEs (CFTE) conducting
PSYOP.

The Warfighting Acquisition University (WarU) (http://www.WarU.edu) is the Congressionally mandated acquisition professional development,
training, and policy research and analysis organization of the Department of War (DoW), under the oversight of the Office of the Under Secretary
of War for Acquisition and Sustainment (OUSW(A&S)). WarU's mission is to equip the acquisition workforce to rapidly accelerate delivery of
warfighter capability through a talent management strategy that includes transformative education, collaborative partnerships, and a continuous
drive for acquisition operational excellence. WarU's vision is: an acquisition workforce operating with wartime urgency, commercial agility, and a
warrior ethos.
WarU provides talent development and continuous professional learning for more than 151,000 warfighting acquisition workforce members, other
DoW professionals, federal civilian agencies, and industry partners to develop, field, and sustain warfighting capability. WarU products and
services target workplace performance, leadership and professionalism, while promoting organizational mission effectiveness.
Additionally, WarU performs research, develops professional publications, offers symposia and frequent topical webinars, and consults on
subjects related to the acquisition functional areas. The FY 2027 request includes funding of 535 civilian full-time equivalents (FTEs), and
operational support to 43 military faculty assigned to WarU.
WarU's main campus is located at Fort Belvoir, Virginia. The University’s structure supports a cross-functional, modernized training methodology
that emphasizes immersive, scenario-based experiential learning focused on portfolio management competencies to optimize the kill chain while
developing dominant decision makers delivered through regional campuses and specialized colleges. WarU has five regional campuses
strategically located in areas with a high concentration of DoW acquisition workforce members. The five regional campuses are:
• Capital and Northeast – Fort Belvoir, Virginia (serves a workforce of 36,070)
• Mid-Atlantic – California, Maryland (serves a workforce of 25,573)
• Midwest – Kettering, Ohio (serves a workforce of 23,034)
• South – Huntsville, Alabama (serves a workforce of 37,330)
• West – San Diego, California (serves a workforce of 29,235)
WarU also has two colleges:

• Defense Systems Management College (DSMC) – Fort Belvoir, Virginia. The DSMC is tasked with offering the global DoW acquisition

management, requirements determination, field training services, leadership, and research.
• College of Contract Management (CCM) – Richmond, Virginia. Located near the Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA)

WarU Core Functions
WarU provides high quality, low-cost training, online resources, and direct support at the point of need to enable the acquisition, requirements
determination, and contingency missions of the DoW (and elements of the Federal Government). WarU’s core functions are defined as:
1. Teaching: Meeting the challenges of the current and forecasted threat environment requires a workforce that is competent and confident
enough to innovate quickly and at scale. WarU instructor-led courses build upon certification training with continuous learning and job
support resources on the WarU platform for developing critical job competencies, innovative thinking, and analytical skills across essential
acquisition functional and leadership roles.
2. Learning Asset Development and Curation: WarU designs, develops, and deploys an expansive portfolio of on-line and instructor-led
courses designed to develop workforce knowledge base and skills to solve complex acquisition problems, manage portfolios, and lead
cross-functional teams to deliver the warfighter a decisive edge. WarU's catalog of self-paced, online learning, including credentials and
topical modules, helps the workforce meet certification requirements and pursue opportunities for career growth. The WarU learning asset
development capability ensures the workforce has the modern content needed to address foundational skills and emerging concepts with
a process that incorporates real-world acquisition lessons learned and uses representative DoW scenarios to hone critical acquisition skills
and confidence to decide and act. Asset development and maintenance are mission critical; moreover, learning content must be
continuously refreshed to foster rapid technology adaptation, at the speed of relevance. In addition, WarU’s category management of
licenses with vendors such as Coursera, LinkedIn Learning, and Percipio, provide workforce members with economical access to
commercial learning assets relevant to non-DoW specific aspects of acquisition, technology, logistics, and leadership.
3. On-Demand Learning: The WarU platform hosts a wide-range of WarU-developed or curated learning assets such as eLearning, “how to”
videos, performance support tools, and web events. The WarU platform offers convenient access for workforce members to maintain
currency, excel at job-related activities and explore emerging concepts. Through webinars and more formal in-person events, WarU helps
the workforce stay up to date on the latest concepts in DoW acquisition and leadership. WarU’s portfolio of online tools—including its
online library, ACQuipedia, and job-support-resources— including the Acquisition Knowledge Matrix, Adaptive Acquisition Framework
pathway resources, and a glossary help the workforce complete critical tasks. The WarU media library also provides a compendium of on-
demand assets.
4. Field Training Services (FTS): WarU’s faculty members use their subject matter expertise to help acquisition program teams and other
customers achieve specific outcomes and improve acquisition outcomes. These include Field Training Teams (FTTs) that provide
comprehensive support to program offices, enhancing their decision-making capabilities across a phase of the acquisition and

The Department of War Civil Military Programs are managed by the Office of the Assistant Secretary of War for Manpower and Reserve Affairs in
the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Personnel and Readiness, and encompass outreach and service programs identified as follows:
• National Guard Youth Challenge Program
• Innovative Readiness Training Program
• DoW STARBASE Program
National Guard Youth Challenge Program: (Title 32 U.S.C. 509) – The National Guard Youth Challenge Program is a youth development and
outreach initiative managed by the Office of the Assistant Secretary of War for Manpower and Reserve Affairs and administered by the National
Guard Bureau through cooperative agreements with participating states. The program provides structured, military-based training and supervised
work experience to help at-risk youth improve life skills, academic achievement, and employment potential.
The program spans 18 months and includes a minimum 22½-week residential phase—beginning with a two-week pre-challenge period—followed
by a 12-month post-residential phase. The program has demonstrated measurable success: participants show higher employment rates,
increased earnings, and greater likelihood of earning a high school diploma, GED, or college credits compared to their peers.
Federal funding may not exceed 75 percent of total operating costs, ensuring shared investment with states. The program currently operates at 32
Youth Challenge and 7 Job Challenge locations across states and territories, including the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico.
Core program components include:
• Helping participants earn a high school diploma or equivalent
• Leadership development, teamwork, and community service
• At select locations, a Job Challenge Phase offering occupational skills training, credentialing, individualized academic and career
counseling, leadership development, and employer engagement

Innovative Readiness Training Program: (Title 10 U.S.C. 2012) – The Innovative Readiness Training Program builds mutually beneficial
partnerships between American communities and the Department of War. The program provides hands-on, mission-essential training for Service
members while addressing public and civil-society needs. Each year, approximately 6,000 to 7,000 joint Service members gain experience in
complex interagency, joint, and total-force environments—conditions that are rarely encountered outside national emergencies and often only
simulated in other training events.
Innovative Readiness Training missions typically include horizontal and vertical construction, infrastructure support, mobile medical and dental
clinics, optometry and veterinary services, and cyber vulnerability assessments. These missions strengthen readiness, enhance community
resilience, and reinforce the connection between the military and the public.
Examples of Fiscal Year 2025 missions include:
• Medical Mission – Operation Healthy Ellwood: From July 20 to August 3, more than 160 joint Service members from four branches and
33 units provided no-cost medical, dental, optometry, veterinary, and behavioral health services in Ellwood City, Pennsylvania. The
mission addressed a critical healthcare gap created by the 2019 closure of the Ellwood City Medical Center. The clinic, located at Lincoln
Junior Senior High School, served over 2,400 patients during its 10-day operation. Service members completed 869 mission-essential
tasks and logged 2,031 training hours, while strengthening civil-military relationships.
• Civil Engineering Mission – Operation Build Eyak: From April 1 to July 12, the Army National Guard, Marine Corps Reserve, and Air
Force Reserve partnered with the Native Village of Eyak in Cordova, Alaska, to support maritime infrastructure development in an area still
affected by the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill. A total of 185 Service members contributed expertise in horizontal construction, civil
engineering planning, and equipment maintenance. Despite challenging terrain and environmental conditions, the team successfully
cleared five acres of land to support construction of a rapid oil-spill response facility. The mission provided an estimated $1 million in
no-cost construction services and delivered 16,470 hours of hands-on training for military engineers.
• Cybersecurity Mission – Cyber Tatanka: From June 1 to June 15, Cyber Tatanka brought together National Guard cyber teams,
international partners, and interagency collaborators to simulate advanced cyber threats and strengthen collective defense capabilities.
More than 150 participants trained through real-time collaboration and scenario-based exercises to enhance readiness for emerging
global cyber challenges.
• Civil Affairs Mission – Operation Outreach Nueces: From July 13 to July 25, the Marine Corps Reserve’s 3rd Civil Affairs Group
partnered with the Nueces County Commissioner’s Office and Texas A&M’s Colonia Program to conduct surveys in underserved colonia
communities along the Texas–Mexico border. Marines completed survey work in 23 of 24 colonias, supporting state grant submissions
and improving community planning. The mission provided more than 1,030 hours of civil affairs training, including public engagement,
data processing, and analysis.

Overview of DCAA
The Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) provides independent audit and financial expertise to ensure every dollar is used effectively to
safeguard our nation’s interests. DCAA operates under the authority, direction, and control of the Under Secretary of War (Comptroller) (USW-C).
Per DoDD 5105.36, perform all necessary contract audits for the Department of War (DoW) and to provide accounting and financial advisory
services regarding contracts and subcontracts to all DoW Components responsible for procurement and contract administration. DCAA’s
capabilities span the entire acquisition lifecycle, from before a contract is awarded to its final closeout. This presence promotes financial integrity at
every stage and assures the DoW maximizes the value of every taxpayer dollar spent on the Warfighter.
Each year, DCAA conducts thousands of audits that provide the basis for recommendations to the acquisition community. In FY 2025, DCAA
identified over $18 billion in total audit exceptions, creating crucial negotiation space for contracting officers by offering critical insight. Auditors
performed 9,527 engagements consisting of 2,480 reports and 7,047 memos, totaling over $788 billion.
Beyond the core audit mission, DCAA provides indispensable advisory and investigative support. These capabilities allow DCAA to proactively
assist acquisition partners and hold contractors accountable, protecting taxpayer dollars across the entire defense enterprise. Tailored advisory
services help contracting officers navigate complex financial issues and negotiate from a position of strength. DCAA supported contracting officers
throughout FY 2025 through advisory services that examined $72 billion in contract costs. These services are tailored to reduce costs and provide
full benefits.
DCAA delivers significant and measurable returns on investment to the American taxpayer. In FY 2025, DCAA examined nearly $788 billion in
contract costs, delivering over $5.3 billion in savings. This demonstrated an impressive $7.50 in savings for every $1 invested in its audit activities.
Alignment with the Department of War priorities
DCAA continues to cultivate the future by supporting the National Defense Strategy objectives of “America First. Peace Through Strength.
Common Sense” and the Secretary of War’s Priorities of Defend the U.S. Homeland, deter China in the Indo-Pacific through Strength not
confrontation, increase burden sharing with U.S Allies and Partners and supercharge the U.S Defense Industrial Base. DCAA audits enable
contracting officials to make necessary investments to ensure the U.S. military remains the strongest and most lethal force in the world. DCAA’s
outreach to defense contractors of all sizes supports the DoW’s policy to accelerate defense procurement and revitalize the defense industrial
base to restore peace through strength.

Mission Specifics
Civilian pay accounts for 85 percent of DCAA’s allocated funds with focuses on:
• DCAA’s audits ensure industry complies with applicable laws, regulations, and contract terms. These audits provide negotiation space,
confidence in contractor capabilities, and maximize value of the DoW dollars spent on weapons systems, services, and supplies to equip
the Warfighter.
• DCAA executed a reorganization to deliver audit expertise with greater speed, precision, and impact. Replacing the legacy regions with
three new mission-focused directorates strategically realigns and embeds DCAA audit teams directly with the military buying commands
they support. Forming the Land Directorate, Sea Directorate, and Air Directorate break down legacy silos, creating unified and flexible
audit teams ready for rapid deployment for the DoW’s most urgent acquisition priorities.
• A Centralized Audit Function (CAF) team was established to focus on complex, high-risk, and enterprise-level audits. This provides robust
oversight into the Department’s largest expenditures, enhancing oversight capability and responsible stewardship of funds.
• DCAA emphasized integration to provide greater flexibility and responsiveness. DCAA’s Field Detachment auditors, those responsible for
the most sensitive work for classified contractors, are now fully integrated into the new directorates. A central Field Detachment Cell
provides dedicated oversight and safeguards for all classified work.
• DCAA provides tailored advisory services to help contracting officers navigate complex financial issues and negotiate from a position of
strength, providing on-demand expertise for better decisions. Key services include direct contract negotiation support, independent
analysis of contractor proposals, advice on pricing and specific cost elements, and assessments of compliance with acquisition
regulations.
• DCAA’s Office of Investigative Support played a critical role detecting and deterring fraud in DoW contracts, providing specialized audit
and financial expertise combating fraud and holding violators accountable. This support contributed to investigations and prosecutions that
recovered over $689.9 million and resulted in 485 months of sentencing along with other sanctions in FY 2025.
• DCAA’s Information Technology and Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO) develops tools to streamline mandatory
contractor financial submissions, automate repetitive manual processes, and leverage the power of data analysis. These tools are
configure and integrate in-house, leveraging existing software, or developed in collaboration with other defense agencies using existing
data stores. This technology-driven approach was instrumental in identifying over $6 billion in funds that could be freed up for more critical
Warfighter needs by reallocating funds, canceling unneeded obligations, and halting a major program extension.

Sustainment (USW(A&S)) as the Principal Staff Assistant. As authorized by Department of Defense Directive 5105.64 and Federal Acquisition
Regulation (FAR) Part 42.302, the DCMA mission is to perform Contract Administration Services (CAS) and Contingency Contract Administration
Services (CCAS) for the Department of War (DOW), other federal agencies, and international partners. This mission ensures taxpayers get what
they pay for and enables the DOW to verify financial statements meet established standards to prevent fraud and ensure regulatory compliance.
The DCMA is the centralized force multiplier for standardized inspection and acceptance of combat weapon systems and payments to the
Defense Industrial Base (DIB). DCMA's acquisition and support professionals are the Department's critical sensor network, providing an essential
link to the DIB through 663 sites in 12 countries. Across a global footprint in 45 countries, they provide administration to over 19,000 contractors,
managing approximately 306,000 active contracts valued at $7.79 trillion. This unique position delivers unparalleled insight to ensure the timely
delivery of warfighting equipment, safeguard taxpayer dollars, and support a healthy industrial base, directly contributing to the strength and
readiness of our armed forces.
The CAS and CCAS workload performed by the workforce enables Military Departments (MILDEPs) and buying commands to increase the on-
time delivery and procurement of critical warfighting equipment at a fair and equitable cost. The DOW weapon system and materiel investments
are key factors that drive DCMA workload throughout the CAS and CCAS acquisition lifecycle.
The DCMA consistently generates a positive annual return on investment (ROI) for DOW and taxpayers significantly, greater than the DCMA’s
annual budget. For every dollar invested in DCMA for FY 2025, DCMA efforts resulted in a ratio of approximately 8.3:1. The DCMA activities such
as litigation, cost and pricing actions, cost rate settlements, workers’ compensation claims, and Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) settlements
returned $9.24 billion to the Department in refunds, recovered costs, forward (future) pricing rates, and negotiated price reductions. The DCMA
has consistently produced a positive ROI for the past seven years, averaging a return of $3.95 for every $1 invested.

Alignment with the Department of War priorities
The DCMA directly supports DOW priorities to enable DOW to remain the world’s preeminent fighting force. The DCMA mission and
responsibilities align with National Defense Strategy (NDS) efforts to; Defend the United States (U.S.) Homeland and supercharge the U.S. DIB.
DCMA workforce performs acquisition life-cycle management activities from pre-award through contract closeout, which include:
• Controlling contractor indirect costs by establishing forward and final rates, resolving claims and disputes, and making final determinations on
cost accounting standard audits.
• Providing negotiation intelligence by providing business system compliance for contract accounting, property management, material
management, earned value and purchasing systems.
• Influencing contract negotiations by making commercial item determinations and providing insight into contract cost and pricing,
approximately 85% of the DCMA workforce are acquisition professionals including production, quality assurance, manufacturing, contracting,
and engineering personnel performing the mission globally.
• Administering DOW awarded contracts through the execution of contract modifications; cost monitoring; managing ground and flight
operations, delivery schedules, and government property; providing transportation authorizations for in-plant material; accepting and
authorizing payments for contracted goods and services; recovering expiring and cancelling funds; and contract close-out.
The DCMA is at the forefront of executing the DOW Security Cooperation mission to build and sustain Allied security interests and industrial
capabilities collaboratively. Within the Security Cooperation community, the DCMA provides support to Foreign Military Sales delegated by the
Service buying commands, Foreign Direct Commercial Sales contracts, and international agreements, which the DCMA directly aligns personnel
to support Allies in critical locations in the U.S. and overseas.
FY 2027 Budget Priorities
The FY 2027 DCMA budget priorities are to implement DOW directives to optimize the value-added support to MILDEPs and buying commands;
streamline processes to gain mission efficiencies; invest strategically in non-labor projects to maximize potential returns on investment; modernize
legacy Information Technology (IT) systems; and leverage advanced IT for greater efficiencies.
Approximately 84% ($1,250.43 million) of the FY 2027 non-cyber budget request supports Agency personnel compensation for the direct funded
full-time equivalent employees. The remaining 16% ($212.56 million) supports the DCMA workforce for critical requirements as: IT network and
modernization, commercial tools, technical refresh and equipment sustainment; facility project renovations, sustainment, and leases;
intragovernmental support for human resource and accounting services; mission travel; Ability One contract closeout and contractor support;
equipment; permanent change of station (household goods storage); and supplies. The DOW continues to invest in new emerging programs and
weapon systems. DCMA continues to leverage automation to effectively align its workforce with its workload and support current and future DOW
investment growth most efficiently.

The Defense Contract Management Agency (DCMA) Cyber budget protects, secures, and defends information and IT systems under its purview
to ensure functional owners and operators have confidence in the confidentiality, integrity, availability, and non-repudiation of the DCMA
information needed to make informed decisions. Some key security principles include isolation; containment; redundancy; layers of defense; least
privilege; situational awareness; and physical or logical segmentation of networks, services, and applications. This budget supports these activities
by providing government and contractor support to prevent unauthorized network access by protecting all information systems, enclaves, and
computing environments from external and internal threats of interception, modification, fabrication, and interruption.
To execute the Department of War's (DoW) Cyber Strategy and protect the warfighter, the DCMA operates through two distinct, mission-focused
cybersecurity entities. First, DCMA IT Cybersecurity Operations (Funding Element 1) is responsible for the internal defense of the agency, tasked
with protecting, securing, and defending all DCMA information and Information Technology (IT) systems. This team maintains a vigilant presence
to deter threats against the agency's own networks and infrastructure. Concurrently, the Defense Industrial Base Cyber Assessment Center
(Funding Element 2) executes an external-facing mission as the DoW's sole entity for conducting cybersecurity assessments of the Defense
Industrial Base, proactively identifying and mitigating vulnerabilities across the contractor supply chain.
FUNDING ELEMENT 1: DCMA IT CYBERSECURITY OPERATIONS
The DCMA IT Cybersecurity Operations mission is to directly support the warfighter by ensuring the operational readiness and security of all
internal DCMA networks and systems. We defend the agency against persistent cyber threats to guarantee confidentiality, integrity, and
availability of critical data used for acquisition, contract management, and mission support. Our defensive cyberspace operations are foundational
to the agency's ability to deliver for the warfighter.
Our budget protects and defends the information and IT systems under DCMA’s purview. DCMA employs key security principles including
isolation, containment, redundancy, least privilege, and network segmentation to build a resilient, multi-layered defense. These principles are put
into action through our 24/7 Defensive Cyberspace Operations, which are critical to mission assurance. These active functions include:
• Proactive Threat Hunting: Actively searching our networks for advanced persistent threats and indicators of compromise that have
bypassed traditional defenses.

FUNDING ELEMENT 2: DEFENSE INDUSTRIAL BASE CYBERSECURITY ASSESSMENT CENTER (DIBCAC)
The Defense Industrial Base Cybersecurity Assessment Center (DIBCAC) is the sole entity entrusted with the Department’s mission of conducting
cybersecurity assessments of defense contractor information systems that process, transmit, or store Controlled Unclassified Information. The
Defense Industrial Base supply chain includes over 220,000 defense contractors and suppliers and is increasingly targeted by capable
adversaries to undermine U.S. national interests. The DIBCAC directly supports the DoD DIB Cybersecurity Strategy mission and vision to ensure
the generation, reliability, and preservation of U.S. warfighting capabilities by protecting sensitive information, operational capabilities, and product
integrity. Furthermore, the DIBCAC assists in Goal 2 of the strategy to “enhance the cybersecurity posture of the DIB” by achieving Objective 2.1,
“evaluate DIB compliance with DoD’s cybersecurity requirements” as the office of primary responsibility for current DoD cybersecurity
assessments and as the office of coordinating responsibility for DoD’s Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification program. The DIBCAC prioritizes
assessments based upon the DoD Sector Risk Management Agency’s list of systemically important entities as required by the National Security
Memorandum 22 and other critical priorities.
The DIBCAC is committed to collaborating with foreign partners to protect Controlled Unclassified Information worldwide. The complex
multinational supply chain and rapidly evolving technology landscape transcends national borders and territories, making ongoing international

The Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) serves as the primary Federal entity for personnel vetting to ensure an effective,
efficient, and trusted workforce for the Federal Government as directed in the Executive Order (E.O.) 13869, as well as the continuation of the
National Industrial Security Program (NISP) mission. The DCSA was formed over the course of 2019 to 2021 and is dedicated to building the best
possible security enterprise to defend the United States. from extant and future adversaries attempting to gain a national security advantage through
the workforce, technologies, and supply chain. Since its formal establishment, DCSA restructured its organization to realign personnel previously
assigned to the disestablished Defense Vetting Directorate to better support and align with the National Defense Strategy by ensuring a trusted
federal, industrial, and affiliated workforce through continuous vetting and insider threat programs. These programs enable government and industry
to deliver uncompromised capabilities to the warfighter by utilizing artificial intelligence, machine learning, and cutting-edge technologies and
innovation. The blending of the operational missions of Industrial Security, Personnel Security, Personnel Vetting, Counterintelligence, Insider
Threat, and professional education and certification provides DCSA with the unique advantage in preserving the nation’s strategic edge. The DCSA
ensures that sensitive and classified U.S. and foreign government information, technologies, and material entrusted to cleared industry are securely
protected. The DCSA, headquartered in Quantico, Virginia, with 165 field offices located across the United States, executes NISP oversight for the
Department of War (DoW) and 35 other Federal executive branch agencies, determines security eligibility for all DoW personnel and conducts
personnel vetting for more than 100 federal agencies. As the Security Training, Education, and Certification functional manager for the DoW, DCSA
provides security education, training, certification, and professional development for DoW and other U.S. Government contractor employees, and
U.S. foreign government partners. The DCSA conducts required NISP assessments to deter, detect, and identify loss or compromise of classified
information and ensure corrective actions are taken to prevent recurrence.
A. Industrial Security (IS) Directorate:
The DCSA Industrial Security Operating Component is responsible for administering the DoW portion of the NISP on behalf of the DoW and
35 federal executive branch agencies that have entered into industrial security agreements.
To implement responsibilities under the NISP, the IS Directorate actively engages with industry and individual members of the Defense
Industrial Base (DIB) on a regular basis, addressing a wide range of issues. These interactions support DCSA's role as the Cognizant
Security Office (CSO) for the DoW in protecting classified information accessed or possessed by cleared facilities. From the initial assessment
and issuance of Facility Clearances (FCL) to enable processing of classified contract requirements, to continuous monitoring and field

oversight., DCSA has made significant improvements. In FY 2025, DCSA reduced overall timelines for granting facility clearances and

The core of the NISP is the Security Review, which DCSA conducts as the CSO within the DoW. These reviews ensure industry compliance
with requirements to protect classified information in classified contracts. Security Reviews evaluate and rate cleared contractors' security
programs to assess compliance with 32 CFR Part 117, using a risk-based approach to determine whether appropriate mitigation measures
are in place to minimize the potential compromise, loss, or damage of classified information. The IS Directorate has increased the number
of Security Reviews through continuous process improvements and the implementation of updated 32 CFR Part 117 policies. Currently,
DCSA reaches approximately 49% of the 9,370 facilities under DoW’s cognizance that require annual assessments. As DCSA continues to
identify and mitigate risks across industry, it refines its oversight methodology, including the Security Review and rating process. This
approach has resulted in the development of a new Security Review score, created in collaboration with industry and government
stakeholders, to effectively implement the policy-designated five-tier rating system. Additionally, DCSA performs Cyber Operational
Readiness Assessments (CORA) on behalf of the DoW for contractors with approved Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRNet)
information systems.
1. National Industrial Security Program
Industrial Security administers the NISP through the granting of FCLs, assessing and mitigating Foreign Ownership, Control, and Influence
(FOCI), the authorization of contractor classified information systems, international security requirements, managing enabling information
systems, and providing Field Operations guidance on oversight.
2. CORA Program
The IS Directorate implements a portion of the CORA program, formerly known as the Command Cyber Readiness Inspection program.
This initiative is mandated by Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff (CJCS). The CORA program enables DCSA to evaluate the cybersecurity
posture of NISP contractors with SIPRNet nodes, thereby enhancing accountability and improving the overall security of the DoD Information
Network (DODIN).
3. Arms, Ammunition, and Explosives (AA&E) Security
The IS Directorate assesses physical security measures for sensitive conventional AA&E at contractor facilities. DCSA’s contributions to the
AA&E program include conducting Pre-Award Security Surveys and annual physical security inspections of U.S. contractor-owned,
contractor-operated facilities that manufacture, test, store, and transport DoW's sensitive conventional AA&E.

The Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) is a critical combat support agency that delivers, operates, and assures the foundational
Command and Control, information sharing capabilities, and global enterprise information infrastructure essential for joint warfighters, national-
level leaders, and coalition partners across the full spectrum of operations.
The DISA Next Strategy directly drives combat support priorities and initiatives, ensuring the delivery of essential capacity and capability for
warfighting information systems. Through planning, engineering, acquisition, testing, fielding, operation, and assurance, DISA develops and
maintains robust information-sharing capabilities, Command and Control solutions, and a global enterprise infrastructure supporting the
Department of War (DoW) and national leadership.

War's priorities: rebuilding the military, reestablishing deterrence, and defending the homeland. By embodying core principles of readiness,
campaigning, continuous modernization, and establishing lethality, DISA ensures the military remains agile and adaptable, capable of rapidly
incorporating new technologies and tactics to counter evolving threats.

outpace evolving threats and drive technological advancements. This ensures a resilient, secure, and scalable network for forces at home and
forward-deployed Combatant Commands (CCMDs). These efforts are crucial to maximizing resilience against foreign adversaries and enabling
seamless interoperability between the Department of War and its allies.

networks, computing infrastructure, and enterprise services. These resources enable critical information sharing and decision-making for the
nation's warfighters and their support elements, directly contributing to national defense. Committed to advancing technology, DISA
strengthens the security and resilience of networks and systems, thereby enhancing current and future U.S. military advantages over
adversaries. Key priority areas include Cybersecurity, National Leadership Command Capability, and White House support.

The Defense Legal Services Agency (DLSA) provides legal advice, services, and support to the Defense Agencies, the Department of War (DoW)
Field Activities, and, as assigned, other organizational entities within the DoW.
DLSA supports litigation involving the Department and other inquiries and requests involving a high volume of documents requiring review. Among
other legal services, the DLSA administers the DoW Standards of Conduct Program; supports and assists the Assistant Secretary of War for
Legislative Affairs in developing the DoW Legislative Program, to include drafting legislation and comments; negotiating on behalf of the DoW
clients with private entities and other Government agencies; ensuring proper use of Government funds and property; providing opinions and
counseling on legal compliance issues; and participating in contractual matters.
The Defense Office of Hearings and Appeals (DOHA) is the largest component of the DLSA, and is responsible for:
• Adjudicating personnel security clearance cases for contractor personnel performing classified work for DOHA-serviced DoW Components
and 30 other Federal Agencies and Departments;
• Conducting personal appearance hearings, and issuing decisions in security clearance and sensitive national security position cases for
DOHA-serviced DoW civilian and military personnel;
• Providing legal reviews, approving statements of reasons, conducting hearings, and issuing decisions in cases under DOHA jurisdiction
requiring trustworthiness decisions for contractor performance of sensitive duties; and,
• Implementing the administrative due-process requirements of Executive Order 10865 (Safeguarding Classified Information Within
Industry) on behalf of the DoW, which serves as the executive agent for the entire Federal Government's implementation of the National
Industrial Security Program.

combatants pursuant to the Military Commissions Act of 2009. There are currently 12 detainees with active charges pending before military

The Defense Prisoners of War/Missing in Action Accounting Agency provides families and the Nation with the fullest possible accounting of
personnel missing from past conflicts. Taxpayer funding supports global search and recovery missions, scientific identification of remains, and
direct communication with families. The agency accounts for those missing from World War II, the Korean War, the Cold War, the Vietnam War,
the Persian Gulf War, the Iraq Theater of Operations, and other conflicts as designated by the Secretary of War. The agency also works with
partner nations, supports U.S. delegations, and strengthens international cooperation to improve accounting outcomes.
Research and Analysis Line of Effort : Research and Analysis is the foundation of every accounting action and relies heavily on coordination
across the agency and with external partners. This work includes building case files, preparing information for families, identifying potential
investigation and recovery sites, and supporting scientific analysis. Research and Analysis collaborates directly with the agency’s laboratories and
the Armed Forces Medical Examiner System by providing the historical, archival, and case-specific information needed for forensic and
anthropological examinations. Coordination with federal agencies, foreign archives, and academic institutions improves data accuracy and
expands access to historical records. These efforts, combined with improvements to the Case Management System, support the agency’s goal of
accounting for more than 200 personnel each year.
Accounting Line of Effort: Accounting activities focus on increasing the number of personnel identified and returned home, with priority on
Vietnam War losses. This work depends on extensive coordination with U.S. embassies, foreign governments, local authorities, and
non-governmental organizations to secure access to sites, obtain permits, and gather information. Taxpayer funding supports investigations,
disinterments, recoveries, and scientific identifications. Even when an individual identification is not possible, families receive all available
information.
Two specialized laboratories are central to the Accounting Line of Effort. These laboratories conduct forensic and anthropological analysis of
remains and artifacts and work closely with the Armed Forces DNA Identification Laboratory and Service Casualty Offices to collect and analyze
DNA samples. Coordination between laboratories, researchers, and field teams ensures that scientific findings are integrated with historical and
investigative information, enabling accurate, science-based identifications and returning loved ones home.
Key projects within the Accounting Line of Effort strengthen the agency’s ability to resolve cases and support coordinated operations. These
include developing accessible personnel files for each missing person as required by 10 U.S.C. § 1509, completing the digitization of Individual

Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment (OUSW(A&S)) and the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Policy (OUSW(P)), leads the
security cooperation enterprise in delivering effective, enduring, and timely solutions that support national security, defense strategic guidance
and mutual U.S. and partner interests.
Consistent with the 2026 National Defense Strategy (NDS), the FY 2027 President’s Budget request continues to align and deliver security
cooperation programs and efforts in accordance with priorities of the President of the United States and Secretary of War’s (SecWar) priorities.
These efforts include the day-to-day operations of the DSCA headquarters, the Defense Security Cooperation University (DSCU), the
Department of War (DoW) Regional Centers for Security Studies, and the Defense Security Cooperation Service (DSCS). Under the provisions
of the Title 10 U.S.C. Chapter 16, the FY 2027 budget request will continue to support the execution of a Department-wide framework for the
assessment, monitoring, and evaluation of security cooperation activities and continue to implement a workforce development program targeting
all DoW professionals supporting security cooperation efforts. The DSCA will continue to execute Department of State security assistance
programs and activities in accordance with the Foreign Assistance Act and the Arms Export and Control Act. Additionally, the DSCA budget
request supports program management and administration of the Humanitarian Assistance, Foreign Disaster Relief, and Humanitarian Mine
Action programs funded within the Overseas Humanitarian, Disaster and Civic Aid appropriation.
The DSCA plans, directs, implements, administers, and provides guidance for the execution of assigned security cooperation programs and
activities and facilitates the planning, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of security cooperation activities funded through the DSCA.
The DSCA activities encourage and enable foreign partners to responsibly act in support of U.S. national security objectives. Security
cooperation activities are often complex and span the phases of conflict from shaping the environment to enabling civil authority activities. The
DSCA collaborates closely with the interagency, geographic combatant commands (CCMD), industry, and partner nations to execute security
cooperation activities. Moreover, the DSCA seeks to maximize security cooperation program effectiveness.

The Defense Technology Security Administration (DTSA), a Field Activity under the Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment, is
the Department of War's (DoW) lead agency for developing and implementing technology security policies for all international transfers of defense-
related goods, services, and technologies. In direct support of the 2026 National Defense Strategy (NDS), the DTSA protects the U.S. military's
critical technological advantages by conducting risk assessments to prevent the diversion of sensitive technology to adversaries while enabling
responsible transfers to allies and partners. The agency works with multilateral export control regimes, chairs the National Disclosure Policy
Committee to support partner interoperability, and plays a critical role in strategic initiatives. Ultimately, the DTSA strives to build enduring
advantages by balancing the safeguarding of critical defense information with fostering a healthy U.S. defense industrial base through its core
functions of national security reviews, international cooperation, policy development, and mission application management.
National Security Review of Defense Information and Technology Transfers:
To protect U.S. technological advantages from nations of concern such as China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, the DTSA leads the national
security review of defense information and technology transfers. In partnership with other government agencies and industry, the DTSA assesses
technology transfer risks associated with Direct Commercial Sales and Foreign Military Sales, makes recommendations on export licenses, and
develops control plans to mitigate those risks.
International Engagements and Security Cooperation:
To strengthen its network of allies and partners, the DTSA collaborates internationally to protect critical defense-related technology, enhance
military interoperability, and promote burden sharing. The agency's leadership conducts direct bilateral engagements to help partners elevate
their technology security and export controls to U.S. standards, building the confidence required for increased cooperation without compromising
America's technological edge.
DoW Export, Technology Release, and Foreign Disclosure Policy Determinations:
As a key function of the DoW the DTSA shapes and implements the policies and regulations that protect U.S. defense information while
facilitating security cooperation with allies.

In a highly competitive security environment with evolving Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD) risks, the Defense Threat Reduction Agency
(DTRA) aligns its efforts with the 2026 National Defense Strategy and focus on "Peace Through Strength," particularly concerning the Indo-Pacific
region. Adversaries like China and Russia are actively expanding and modernizing their nuclear and chemical, biological, radiological, and
nuclear (CBRN) capabilities, while nations such as Iran and North Korea pursue advanced technologies that undermine regional and global
stability. In response, DTRA's FY 2027 President’s Budget request prioritizes investments to protect the U.S. homeland and counter these WMD
risks, enabling the Department of War (DoW), the U.S. Government (USG), and international partners to deter strategic attacks, prevent
proliferation, and prevail in any potential conflict.
As a Combat Support Agency, the DTRA provides cross-cutting solutions to enhance warfighter lethality and defend the homeland, primarily
focusing on China's WMD threats while also addressing other high-risk regional destabilizers. The agency executes its mission through five core
functions: ensuring a reliable strategic deterrent, developing technical capabilities for the warfighter, reducing CBRN threats through risk reduction
and partner capacity building, providing strategic and operational support with subject matter expertise, and assisting the Joint Force with plans
and solutions to address CBRN risks. The DTRA's funding enables critical activities such as force-on-force exercises, mission assurance
assessments, and direct support to Combatant Commands, ensuring a robust posture to deter and respond to WMD and emerging CBRN threats
in crisis and conflict.
NONPROLIFERATION ACTIVITIES
As a key component of nonproliferation, the DTRA enhances global stability by executing U.S. arms control treaties and agreements. DTRA’s
activities focus on building confidence in agreement compliance through the inspection, monitoring, and verification of weapons stockpiles. The
agency's role extends to post-conflict stabilization operations and the training of international law enforcement and border personnel in various
regions, including the former Soviet Union, Europe, Asia, and Africa. By controlling, safeguarding, and eliminating existing weapons, DTRA's arms
control mission is a focal point for U.S. efforts to reduce the threat from WMD and directly enhances national security interests.
The DTRA's implementation of arms control agreements involves three main objectives: conducting inspections of foreign facilities, escorting
foreign inspection teams within the U.S. and at its overseas facilities, and developing the necessary technology to ensure compliance. The agency
trains and deploys teams to exercise U.S. treaty rights for agreements such as the Plutonium Production Reactor Agreement, Vienna Document
2011, Dayton Peace Agreement, and the Chemical Weapons Convention. Furthermore, the DTRA operates monitoring stations for the

The United States faces a highly competitive security environment characterized by evolving weapons of mass destruction (WMD) risks across
multiple domains. Consistent with the National Security Strategy, the National Defense Strategy (NDS), and FY 2027-2031 Defense Planning
Guidance (DPG), focused on Peace Through Strength, the Defense Threat Reduction Agency (DTRA) is aligned to counter threats with a focus on
the Indo-pacific region. China and Russia are expanding and modernizing their nuclear forces, diversifying advanced conventional WMD delivery
systems, and actively developing chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) capabilities that directly threaten the homeland and
American security. At the same time, Iran and North Korea are pursuing advanced warfighting capabilities to undermine regional security and
global stability in ways that pose considerable risk to U.S. objectives. Additionally, the potential for the intentional or accidental release of
biological pathogens or hazardous chemicals contribute to a dynamic CBRN threat environment.
DTRA’s Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 budget request reflects the continued focus on strengthening the agency’s alignment to the Secretary of War’s
priorities. It invests in delivering the capabilities required to protect the Homeland and counter WMD risks while enabling the Department of War
(DoW), the United States Government (USG), and international partners (through burden sharing) to deter strategic attacks against the United
States and its Allies; prevent WMD and emerging CBRN threats; and prevail against WMD-armed adversaries in crisis and conflict.
DTRA enables the DoW, the USG, and selected allies to meet U.S. national security goals through deterrence, enhancing warfighter lethality, and
defending the Homeland. DTRA aligns operations, activities, and investments primarily focused on China’s WMD threats, but also addresses other
adversaries and high-risk regional destabilizers. In its role as both a Defense Agency and Combat Support Agency, DTRA provides cross-cutting
solutions to support each of these mission priorities. DTRA is committed to achieving concrete outcomes and strategic effects through its five core
functions:
• Ensuring a reliable, resilient strategic deterrent through nuclear surety, mission assurance, and crisis response activities;
• Developing and delivering technical capabilities to the warfighter across the WMD threat spectrum;
• Preventing, reducing, and eliminating CBRN threats through targeted and focused risk reduction, arms control, partner capacity building
and warfighter support;
• Providing strategic and operational support through subject matter expertise, technical reach back, tailored analysis, and exercise support;
• Supporting the Joint Force with plans, concepts, exercises, and materiel solutions to address CBRN operational and strategic risks.

The Department of War Education Activity (DoWEA) provides schooling for children of U.S. military families stationed around the world. DoWEA’s
purpose is to ensure students receive a consistent, high-quality education that prepares them to succeed as responsible citizens. DoWEA
operates under the Department of War and includes the overseas school system, the domestic school system, Management Headquarters, and
Consolidated School Support.
The overseas school system educates 44,779 students in 106 schools across 11 countries: Bahrain, Belgium, Cuba, Germany, Italy, Japan,
Korea, the Netherlands, Spain, Turkey, and the United Kingdom. These schools provide a full Pre-K through 12th-grade program and oversee the
Department’s Virtual High School, which offers online courses to support academic and career goals. Performance is measured through student
achievement, graduation rates, and the ability to maintain continuous school operations in overseas environments.
The domestic school system serves 21,591 students in 53 schools across seven states—Alabama, Georgia, Kentucky, New York, North Carolina,
South Carolina, and Virginia—as well as Guam and Puerto Rico. The program also manages Special Arrangement contracts that fund tuition and
transportation for 1,195 students in locations where the Department does not operate its own schools. These agreements, authorized under Title
10, U.S. Code § 2164, allow local public school districts to educate eligible military-connected students. Current Special Arrangement locations
include Delaware, Massachusetts, New York, and Puerto Rico. Performance is tracked through accurate enrollment, timely tuition payments, and
continuity of student services.
The Non-DoW Schools Program supports 4,999 students whose families serve in remote overseas areas without Department-run schools. Eligible
students receive tuition assistance and other required educational support. The program operates under statutory authority in Title 20, U.S. Code
§ 926(b). Performance is measured through timely tuition processing, verification of student eligibility, and compliance reviews to ensure students
receive appropriate educational services.
Management Headquarters provides system-wide oversight and ensures all schools follow a consistent Pre-K through 12 curriculum. Funding
supports curriculum development, professional development for educators, program evaluations, and monitoring of student performance.
Performance is assessed through accreditation results, curriculum implementation milestones, and educator training completion rates.

The Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation (OLDCC), statutorily authorized under Title10 United States Code (U.S.C.) §198, is a unique
Department of War (DoW) field activity that furthers the Secretary’s priorities by supporting efforts to enhance the readiness and lethality of military
installations, ranges, and test facilities. These efforts in turn help support the States, defense communities, warfighters, and their families. In
accordance with Title 10 U.S.C. §2391 and numerous National Defense Authorization and DoW Appropriation Acts, the OLDCC provides
assistance to States, counties, municipalities, regions, and other communities to foster cooperation with military installations to enhance the
military mission, achieve facility and infrastructure savings and reduced operating costs, address encroachment and compatible land use issues,
support military families, and increase military, civilian, and industrial readiness and resiliency.
The OLDCC often engages at the juxtaposition of State and local civilian efforts in response to local mission activity and/or need, embodying the
Secretary’s priorities to restore the warrior ethos, rebuild our military, and reestablish deterrence.
DoW facilities and the industrial base rely upon the States and communities that host them, a circumstance where the readiness and resilience of
installations and the industrial base are intrinsically related to their neighboring civilian jurisdictions, especially where dependencies exist on public
infrastructure and services. The OLDCC continuum of technical and financial assistance enables these State and community partners to
organize, plan, and carry out efforts that benefit both them and DoW installations, the organic industrial base, and the defense industrial
base.
On behalf of the Secretary of War, the OLDCC also directs and executes the Defense Economic Adjustment Program, coordinating the
involvement of other Federal Agencies through the Economic Adjustment Committee (EAC) per Executive Order 12788 (Defense Economic
Adjustment Program), as amended by Executive Order 13378 (Amendments to Executive Order 12788 Relating to the Defense Economic
Adjustment Program). The OLDCC Director is the Executive Director for the Economic Adjustment Committee, and provides guidance and
assistance in leveraging other Federal agency expertise and resources to enable the DoW, its Components, and affected States and communities
to: 1) assess economic and socioeconomic hardships caused by DoW program changes; 2) identify and evaluate alternative responses for local
economic recovery; 3) identify resource requirements; and 4) assist in the preparation and implementation of adjustment strategies or action
plans. The Departments of Labor and Commerce are each co-vice chairs of the Economic Adjustment Committee. For example, DoW Indo-
Pacific basing actions are complemented by the OLDCC-led Economic Adjustment Committee efforts along with the Territory of Guam’s Office of
the Governor and its legislature, resulting in the execution of approximately $233 million in outside-the-fence infrastructure investments.

Programs of Assistance:
OLDCC Programs of Assistance are continually scrutinized to ensure they effectively enable communities to be responsive to DoW needs as they
support the military and civilian households (over 70% of the military households reside off installation) that sustain the local mission. These
programs presently include: Installation Readiness (which encompasses OLDCC Compatible Use activities); Mission Growth (including support for
our Indo-Pacific basing actions); Defense Community Infrastructure; Modernization; Public Schools on Military Installations; and Mission
Realignment (including Base Closures and Realignments). These programs help states and communities respond to a range of need, including
mitigating threats to the installation-level operating environment; DoW mission changes; and demand for increased public services and
infrastructure with a focus on civilian Critical Infrastructure risk management.
Installation Readiness:
These efforts are the only DoW source of technical and financial assistance for states and communities to work with nearby installations (including
testing and training ranges, special use airspace, military operations areas, and/or military training routes) to plan, enhance infrastructure, and
implement measures that contribute to maintaining or enhancing a military installation’s readiness and lethality while also supporting the warfighter
mission.
Installation Readiness activities are geared to support the organizing, planning, and implementation actions necessary to avoid, prepare for,
minimize the effect of, adapt to, and recover from extreme weather events, or from anticipated or unanticipated changes in environmental
conditions, that do, or have the potential to, adversely affect the lethality of a military installation, assessing potential impacts to critical
infrastructure, and designing risk management enhancements / mitigations in order to maintain, improve, or rapidly reestablish installation mission
assurance and mission-essential functions. Under this assistance, State or local governmental entities analyze external threats and vulnerabilities
to the readiness and lethality of the installation, develop mitigation strategies, and identify resources necessary to ensure the continuity of DoW
and installation mission capabilities. This program enables a collaborative response that leverages Federal, State, local, and private resources to
optimize the capacities and funds that each can bring to the effort. These program activities establish or reinforce an ongoing collaboration
between civilian (public and private) and military equities that thrives beyond the term of any project. Installation Readiness projects may include a
comprehensive review of threats and vulnerabilities; targeted studies or plans concerning, but not limited to, transportation, land
use/encroachment, utility services, housing, stormwater management, and other critical infrastructure. Applicants are encouraged to undertake
tabletop exercises with their local installations and other key partners, including State National Guard, to facilitate threat-based scenarios to
identify critical infrastructure vulnerabilities and prioritize improvements where the need exists. OLDCC is currently supporting 89 active efforts
serving the readiness needs of the Department through the development of plans to identify and then carry out efforts to prevent encroachment

The Washington Headquarters Services (WHS) FY 2027 President’s Budget request of $536,546 thousand is $126,440 thousand above the FY
2026 requested amount and is comprised of $6,956 thousand in pricing increases and a net $119,484 thousand in programmatic increases. The
FY 2027 request empowers the WHS to continue to support key administration initiatives and priorities in defense of the Nation.
The WHS directly supports the Department of War (DoW), the Secretary of War (SECWAR), the Office of the Secretary of War (OSW), the Deputy
Secretary of War (DEPSECWAR), the Defense Legal Services Agency (DLSA), the United States Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces
(USCAAF), the Defense Agencies and DoW Field Activities (DAFA), including Pentagon Force Protection Agency (PFPA), the Defense Security
Cooperation Activity (DSCA), the Defense Prisoner of War (POW)/Missing in Action (MIA) Accounting Agency (DPAA), National Guard Bureau,
Defense Technology Security Administration (DTSA), and Defense Test Resource Management Center (DTRMC) and other select Federal
Agencies such as the Department of State (DoS), the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), and the White House. Additionally
beginning in FY 2026 WHS began supporting the Direct Reporting Program Managers (DRPM) including the DRPM for Submarines, DRPM for
Golden Dome for America, DRPM for Critical Major Weapons Systems, as well as the Economic Defense Unit. The WHS provides more than 80
essential services, absorbing and consolidating administrative requirements that allow DoW staff to focus on matters involving policy analysis and
program oversight more efficiently. The WHS demonstrates expertise and innovation and provides solutions to tackle complex issues though
operational prioritization. The WHS continues to transform into an organization of the future by focusing and upgrading core functions.
The WHS continues to cultivate the future by investing in the 2026 National Defense Strategy (NDS) objectives of “America First. Peace Through
Strength. Common Sense,” through the following lines of effort:
1) Defend the Homeland – The WHS provides foundational, mission-critical support that enhances the operational readiness and
effectiveness of supported stakeholders directly responsible for homeland defense.
2) Deter China in the Indo-Pacific Through Strength, Not Confrontation – The WHS is a key enabler for supported stakeholders that manage
strategic alliances, technology security, and inter-agency coordination, all of which are central to the deterrence strategy in the Indo-
Pacific.
3) Increase Burden-Sharing with U.S. Allies and Partners – The WHS streamlines administrative and support functions in support of the
Department by efficiently allocating and maximizing resources, consistently innovating solutions, and providing a skilled workforce.

WASHINGTON HEADQUARTERS SERVICES IMMEDIATE OFFICE:
The WHS Immediate Office (WHS IO) serves as the Agency integrator and establishes the framework for synchronizing emergent, cross-
functional requirements among WHS Directorates to secure mission accomplishment and achieve strategic goals on behalf of the WHS Director
and the Director of Administration and Management (DA&M). The WHS IO provides program management, administrative, and operational
services to sustain and meet new Administration and regulatory requirements and supports Presidential and DoW transitions.
ACQUISITION DIRECTORATE:
The Acquisition Directorate (AD) plans, coordinates, and manages an extensive range of supplies and professional services totaling $4.377 billion
in obligations in FY 2025. The AD is the single enterprise contracting office supporting acquisition services to all OSW components, WHS, the
PFPA, the DSCA, the DPAA, and more. Contracts for knowledge-based services, research and development, and facility support account for
more than 80 percent of AD’s total obligations, providing a consistent capability to connect people and process information.
EXECUTIVE SERVICES DIRECTORATE:
The Executive Services Directorate (ESD) provides comprehensive knowledge management, information security, and visual information services
to the OSW and DAFAs. The ESD also executes legally mandated programs and supports the Pentagon Reservation by providing a wide variety
of customer services. The ESD provides executive services and a wide range of history and library services to the SECWAR, DEPSECWAR,
OSW components, the Joint Staff and the DAFAs, and other agencies and organizations. Mandated programs include the Freedom of Information
Act, the Privacy Act of 1974, the Federal Records Act, the Paperwork Reduction Act, Executive Order 13526, and programs relating to

The Cooperative Threat Reduction (CTR) Program enables the Department of War (DoW) to work cooperatively with partner nations to reduce or eliminate the
threat of the proliferation of Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD) or WMD-related materials. The DoW derives authority to carry out the CTR Program through the
Cooperative Threat Reduction Act (Public Law 113-291), and has used this authority to reduce chemical, biological, and nuclear threats to the United States and
its interests worldwide. To accomplish this, the CTR Program includes several lines of effort: the Biological Threat Reduction Program, the Proliferation Prevention
Program, Global Nuclear Security, Chemical Security Program (formerly Chemical Security and Elimination); and Transportation Elimination Disposition (formerly

partner nations to prevent, detect, and prepare for the threat of biological weapons use by an adversary. The program implements activities to prevent the
proliferation of biological weapons; biological weapons components; and biological weapons-related materials, technologies, and expertise. To achieve its national
security mission, the program assists partner nations as they seek to improve their biosafety and biosecurity capabilities to counter biological threats. The BTRP
works cooperatively with countries across Africa, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia to secure pathogen collections and enhance biosafety and biosecurity at
vulnerable sites. The BTRP goals for each partner country and region follow.

The Overseas Humanitarian, Disaster, and Civic Aid (OHDACA) appropriation supports the Secretary of War and the combatant
commanders to employ humanitarian programs as strategic tools that directly support national and theater strategies to build partner nation
resilience, capacity and capability; expand and strengthen alliances; advance DoW access and operational readiness; counter malign
actors; and promote burden-sharing. OHDACA-funded security cooperation programs include Humanitarian Assistance (HA), Humanitarian
Mine Action (HMA), and DoW support to U.S. Government Foreign Disaster Relief (FDR). Together, these programs build civil capabilities
and reinforce DoW and U.S. national security objectives by addressing critical vulnerabilities before they become security challenges.
OHDACA activities build partner nation capacity and capabilities to provide essential health and education services to their
populations, respond to humanitarian crises, and build resilience against trans-border threats. Enabling burden sharing with allies
and partners reduces the need for the U.S. to respond to crises abroad, allowing the Joint Force to stay focused on core warfighting
priorities—particularly deterring China and preparing for high-end conflict.
By strengthening our partners’ capacity and capabilities to address fundamental humanitarian needs, and to prepare for, and respond
to disasters, OHDACA-funded activities are reducing the reliance on and the ultimate costs to American taxpayers, while improving
DoW’s access and ability to operate in strategically important locations.
Humanitarian Assistance Program: Developed jointly with partner nation authorities, DoW’s HA program builds capacity of partner nation
civilian institutions by improving disaster risk reduction mitigation and preparedness; basic infrastructure support (e.g., water, sanitation, and
shelter); basic education; and public health in support of U.S. security priorities. OHDACA-funded HA activities include HA construction,
training, and equipping projects, donating non-lethal DoW excess property for humanitarian purposes, and transporting private humanitarian
donations to achieve national security priorities.
DoW HA activities bolster a partner nation’s capacity to reduce the risk of, prepare for, mitigate the consequences of, and respond to
humanitarian disasters, including health threats, thereby ensuring an independent and capable partner. They also build partner nation
resilience against the influence of malign strategic competitors and transnational threats to security and stability and make our partners

The combatant commands (CCMDs) leverage OHDACA-funded security cooperation HA as a highly effective military-to-civilian program
that complements other security cooperation tools. By delivering tangible benefits to civilian populations and governments, these programs
foster trust, build enduring relationships, and expand U.S. military access in key strategic regions. They also improve partner nations’
abilities to respond to crises domestically and regionally, reducing the need for U.S. assistance and preserving Joint Force focus on core
warfighting missions.
Humanitarian Mine Action Program: The OHDACA-funded HMA program enables partner nations across the globe to independently
manage and mitigate threats to civilian populations posed by the presence of explosive remnants of war (ERW) or unexploded
ordnance (UXO) via HMA train-the-trainer missions.
The DoW HMA Program assists partner nation civilian populations plagued by landmines, explosive ERW, and the hazardous effects
of unexploded ordnance to develop indigenous capacity for humanitarian demining, explosive ordnance disposal (including
underwater), and safe management of stockpiled conventional munitions. The program trains partner nation demining cadres to
identify suspected contaminated areas, conduct surveys and assessments, destroy landmines and ERW, and return cleared areas for
civilian use. It also provides humanitarian demining supplies and equipment to partner nations for training on the clearance of
contaminated areas to allow the repatriation of internally displaced persons and/or refugees.
U.S. forces provide training and support in the disposal, demilitarization, physical security, and stockpile management of potentially
dangerous stockpiles of explosive ordnance, small arms, and light weapons, including man-portable air defense systems. In addition
to providing CCMDs with access to areas otherwise not readily available, this security cooperation program contributes to DoW, unit,
and individual U.S. operational readiness by providing unique deployment opportunities to hone critical wartime, civil-military, language,
and cultural skills.
Directly supporting the HMA Program, the Humanitarian Demining Training Center in Virginia, is the DoW center for the training of
deploying U.S. military personnel for humanitarian mine action missions. The Humanitarian Demining Training Center incorporates
new demining technologies and techniques into training plans and provides current data on country-specific ERW (including UXO,
mines, booby traps, and small arms ammunition) in support of training. The Humanitarian Demining Training Center training includes
the preparation and delivery of instruction in humanitarian landmine and battle area clearance, explosive ordnance disposal, stockpiled
conventional munitions assistance, underwater ERW clearance, and casualty care.
Foreign Disaster Relief: The DoW is postured to support the U.S. government’s disaster relief activities outside the United States and its
territories, typically in response to a formal request from the Department of State when DoW provides unique military capabilities to save
lives and alleviate the immediate suffering of foreign disaster victims. DoW FDR supports these activities when directed by the President or

The Operational Forces compose the core element of the Marine Corps, which is the Marine Air Ground Task Force (MAGTF). The MAGTF is a scalable, task organized force
generation construct that permits a composite assembly of forces from the four MAGTF elements—Command Element (CE), Ground Combat Element (GCE), Logistics Combat
Element (LCE), and Aviation Combat Element (ACE)—to rapidly deploy ready forces in support of combatant commanders. The scalable nature of the MAGTF offers tiered force
and capability levels and provides a continuous forward presence via a Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU), an amphibious capable and self-sustainable Marine Expeditionary
Brigade (MEB), an enduring middleweight Marine Expeditionary Force (MEF), or a Special-Purpose MAGTF (SPMAGTF). The MAGTF is a balanced force structure that allows
it to respond to the full spectrum of conflicts across the globe, from conventional to irregular warfare, anti-access/area denial to regional deterrence, and security cooperation
exercises to humanitarian relief. The Operational Forces sub-activity group funds training and routine operations; maintenance and repair of organic ground equipment; official
travel, including travel for reservists mobilized under 12304b authority for active component requirements; information technology repair and replacement; and
replenishment/replacement of unit and individual equipment and supplies in order to meet the Commandant of the Marine Corps Title X responsibilities to train, equip, and deploy
ready forces in support of national security interests. Additionally, the Operational Forces sustain unique capabilities that provide special operations-capable forces to
Commander, US Special Operations Command (USSOCOM).

The Field Logistics sub-activity group resources weapon systems' lifecycle management and sustainment, weapon systems' acquisitions technical support, quality assurance
overview, and service-wide provisioning implementations. Additionally, Field Logistics resources research, design, and development of Marine Corps personal protective
equipment. Systems and programs within this group are categorized by Joint Capability Area (JCA). JCAs are collections of similar Department of War (DoW) activities
functionally grouped to support capability analysis, strategy development, investment decision making, capability portfolio management, and capabilities-based force development
and operational planning.
Battlespace Awareness: The ability to sense, understand, and orchestrate observables affecting the operational environment to enable national and military decision making.
Battlespace Awareness includes the following major capability areas: Sensing; Human Intelligence; Counterintelligence; Signals Collections; Imagery Collections; Planning and
Directions; Biometrics; and Processing and Exploitations.
Command and Control: The ability to exercise authority and direction by a properly designated commander or decision maker over assigned and attached forces and resources in
the accomplishment of the mission. Command and Control includes the following major capability areas: Planning and Direction; Gathering; Extraction; Dissemination;
Counterintelligence; and Digitally Literate Workforce.
Force Application: The ability to integrate the use of maneuver and engagement in all environments to create the effects necessary to achieve mission objectives. Force
Application includes the following major capabilities: Maneuver to Engage; Maneuver to Insert; and Maneuver to Secure.
Force Support: The ability to establish, develop, maintain, and manage a mission ready Total Force. Force Support includes the following major capability areas: Force
Management and Force Application Employment.
Logistics and Sustainment: The ability to project and sustain a logistically ready joint force through the deliberate sharing of national and multi-national resources to effectively
support operations, extend operational reach and provide the joint force commander the freedom of action necessary to meet mission objectives. Logistics and Sustainment
includes the flowing major capability areas: Deployment and Distribution; Supply and Equipment Management; Equipment Maintenance; Logistics Services; Operational Contract
Support; Health Services; Base and Installation Support; Facilities, Sustainment, Restoration, and Modernization for maintenance and repairs of facilities; and Engineering.
Joint Information: The ability to share and protect information across DoW and with mission partners coupled with the ability to generate, project, preserve, or deny access to
information to improve understanding, decision making, and communication and to affect the perceptions, attitudes, decision making, and behavior of relevant actors. Joint
information includes the following major capability areas: Information Transport; Network Management; Enterprise Services; Generation; Preservation; Denial; Human Aspects of
Military Operations; and Military Information Support Operations.
Civilian Personnel: Civilian personnel provide program, contract, information technology, engineering, financial, supply, logistics services, and management to the portfolios of
field logistics programs.
